analysis.one_liner: Repeals railroad workers' right to sue employers for negligence, moving injury claims into state workers' compensation programs.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in October 1990 with no cosponsors, died in the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Federal Employers' Liability Act (FELA), the 1908 law that lets railroad workers sue their employer for injuries caused by negligence, with damages decided by a jury. Instead, every injured railroad worker would file a claim under their state's no-fault workers' compensation system, like most other workers. The bill would also force states to open their workers' compensation programs to railroad employees, and it would make Amtrak pay state workers' compensation taxes and fees like any other employer.
analysis.who_benefits: Railroad companies gain the most: they would no longer face fault-based lawsuits, where juries can award large damages for employer negligence and where the threat of liability pressures railroads on safety. Injured workers would gain a guaranteed, no-fault benefit for any job injury, without having to prove the railroad was at fault. Amtrak would gain access to state systems but would also have to start paying state workers' compensation taxes and assessments it is currently exempt from.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Federal Employers' Liability Act of 1908, ending the fault-based system in which railroad workers must prove employer negligence to recover damages and in which awards can be reduced if the worker was partly at fault.

It requires every state to let railroad employees into the state workers' compensation program and to treat their injury, death, and occupational disease claims the same as any other worker's claim, overriding state laws that currently exclude railroad workers.
The bill's own findings argue that fault-based compensation fails to pay all injured workers, produces lengthy litigation with high transaction costs, and burdens both courts and the industry.
It subjects Amtrak to state workers' compensation taxes, fees, and assessments in the same way as any other interstate entity doing business in a state.

analysis.who_pays: Injured railroad workers and their families. FELA jury verdicts for serious injuries, and the negotiating leverage they create in settlements, are generally worth far more than scheduled state workers' compensation benefits. Repealing FELA would also remove the industry-specific financial pressure on railroads to prevent negligent injuries. Workers' compensation would still pay something for every injury, but typically at state-set rates with no jury and no damages for pain, lost future earnings beyond statutory caps, or employer fault.
analysis.who_pays_short: Injured railroad workers and their families

drawbacks.text: Railroad workers would lose the right to a jury trial and to full fault-based damages. Under FELA, a worker who proves the railroad's negligence can recover compensation for the full extent of the harm; state workers' compensation schedules typically pay fixed, and often much lower, amounts regardless of how badly the employer behaved.

Repealing employer liability for negligence removes the strongest financial disincentive railroads have to invest in safety. The bill's own text concedes the fault system creates incentives tied to 'railroad safety' that the no-fault approach would eliminate, without replacing them with any new safety enforcement mechanism.

Benefit levels would vary by state, since the bill leaves benefit schedules to each state. A worker's compensation for the same injury would depend on where the railroad employs them, and some state programs are notoriously low.

The bill gives railroads a competitive advantage the findings describe openly: other transport modes already operate under state workers' compensation, and the bill frames repealing FELA as relieving railroads of a burden on interstate commerce, a cost reduction that flows to railroad operators rather than to workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has a real appeal: guaranteed no-fault benefits for every injured railroad worker, with faster and cheaper processing than court litigation, and the bill's findings make a sincere case that fault-based compensation leaves some injured workers with nothing. But the trade it offers is heavily one-sided. Workers would give up their single most powerful remedy, the negligence lawsuit with jury-determined damages, in exchange for state-set benefit schedules that are usually worth less, while railroads shed a century of liability exposure and lose a major market incentive for safety. A fairer version would have paired FELA repeal with federal minimum benefit standards or a dedicated railroad compensation fund; this bill has neither. As written, the design mainly shifts costs from railroad balance sheets onto injured workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last weeks of the 101st Congress with zero cosponsors and sat in the Labor and Human Resources Committee until the Congress ended on January 3, 1991, with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Kasten introduced the bill on October 17, 1990, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
No cosponsors signed on from either party.
The committee took no further action, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

The bill would have repealed the Federal Employers' Liability Act and required all claims for railroad work-related injuries accruing after enactment to be processed under state workers' compensation programs, with pre-enactment claims continuing under FELA.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Railroad workers and their unions are better off: the fault-based right to sue railroads for negligent injuries survived intact, and railroads did not get the liability relief they have long sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Railroad workers, who kept their right to sue

for.name: Sen. Robert W. Kasten, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 17, 1990, near the end of the Congress.

for.name: Railroad industry
for.what_they_did: Railroads have long sought to replace FELA's fault-based litigation with no-fault systems; the bill's findings adopt industry arguments that FELA burdens the industry against competing transport modes and raises costs.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Edward Kennedy, D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill never left committee.

against.name: Railroad labor unions
against.what_they_did: Railroad unions have consistently defended FELA as the protection that lets workers recover full damages for employer negligence, and have opposed every repeal effort.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and no votes were ever recorded, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Railroads (freight and passenger carriers, including Amtrak)
industries.note: Repealing FELA would end jury-determined negligence damages, the industry's largest injury-related cost, and replace it with predictable state premiums. The gain comes directly out of injured workers' recoveries, and the bill would also strip Amtrak's exemption from state workers' compensation taxes and assessments.

industries.industry: Workers' compensation insurers and state funds
industries.note: Railroads forced into state systems would pay premiums or assessments to state funds and private carriers, adding a large new block of covered employers. The gain comes from railroad payments, not from workers.

industries.industry: Plaintiff-side trial lawyers and claimant representatives
industries.note: FELA contingency-fee litigation is a major line of work for claimant attorneys; moving claims into administrative workers' compensation processes would largely eliminate it. Their interest runs with railroad workers'.
